topics.title: Perimeter: Measure and calculate perimeter of rectangles and irregular shapes using mm, cm and m
Millimetres: Measure with millimetres; convert between mm, cm and m using scaled instruments

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate for the length of an ironing board?
questions.hint: Compare each unit with a 30 cm school ruler: 115 mm is only 11.5 cm (too short), and 115 m is longer than a football field (too long)!

keyPoints.note: Use benchmarks: 10 mm = 1 cm, a school ruler = 30 cm, 100 cm = 1 m.
Compare each unit with a 30 cm school ruler: 115 mm is only 11.5 cm (too short), and 115 m is longer than a football field (too long)!

steps.explain: Convert 115 mm to centimetres by dividing by 10: 115 mm = 11.5 cm, which is shorter than a pencil — far too small for an ironing board.

steps.explain: Check 115 cm: since 100 cm = 1 m, 115 cm is 1.15 m (just over 1 metre long), which matches a real ironing board.

steps.explain: Check 115 m and 115 km: 115 m is longer than a soccer field, and 115 km is the distance between cities — both are far too large.
steps.work: \(115\text{ m and } 115\text{ km are far too long}\)

steps.explain: Therefore, 115 cm is the best estimate for the length of an ironing board.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate for the length of a small car?
questions.hint: Remember 1 m = 100 cm (a big adult stride). A small car is about 4 metres long.

keyPoints.note: Use benchmarks: 10 mm = 1 cm, a school ruler = 30 cm, 100 cm = 1 m.
Remember 1 m = 100 cm (a big adult stride). A small car is about 4 metres long.

steps.explain: Check 4 mm and 4 cm: 4 mm is the thickness of a coin stack and 4 cm is about the width of two fingers — far too small for a real car.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 172" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:442px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="0" y="0" width="340" height="172" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="170" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Small car</text><path d="M55,105 L65,78 L115,58 L215,58 L258,78 L285,84 L285,112 L55,112 Z" fill="#f87171" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="118,64 166,64 166,82 95,82" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><polygon points="174,64 212,64 242,82 174,82" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="105" cy="112" r="18" fill="#1e293b"/><circle cx="105" cy="112" r="8" fill="#cbd5e1"/><circle cx="235" cy="112" r="18" fill="#1e293b"/><circle cx="235" cy="112" r="8" fill="#cbd5e1"/><line x1="55" y1="40" x2="285" y2="40" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/><polygon points="55,40 63,36 63,44" fill="#2563eb"/><polygon points="285,40 277,36 277,44" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="170" y="162" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#0369a1">Eliminate units that are too small</text></svg>

steps.explain: Check 4 m: 4 metres equals 400 cm (about 4 big strides), which is the realistic length of a small family car.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 172" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:442px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="0" y="0" width="340" height="172" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="170" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Small car</text><path d="M55,105 L65,78 L115,58 L215,58 L258,78 L285,84 L285,112 L55,112 Z" fill="#f87171" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="118,64 166,64 166,82 95,82" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><polygon points="174,64 212,64 242,82 174,82" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="105" cy="112" r="18" fill="#1e293b"/><circle cx="105" cy="112" r="8" fill="#cbd5e1"/><circle cx="235" cy="112" r="18" fill="#1e293b"/><circle cx="235" cy="112" r="8" fill="#cbd5e1"/><line x1="55" y1="40" x2="285" y2="40" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/><polygon points="55,40 63,36 63,44" fill="#2563eb"/><polygon points="285,40 277,36 277,44" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="170" y="162" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="12.5" font-weight="700" fill="#0369a1">4 m = 400 cm (realistic car length)</text></svg>

steps.explain: Check 4 km: 4 kilometres is 4000 m, which is a long driving distance, not the length of a car.
Therefore, 4 m is the best estimate for the length of a small car.

questions.stem: Which is the best estimate for the length of a birthday card?
questions.hint: Compare with a 30 cm school ruler: a birthday card is a bit more than half the length of a 30 cm ruler.

keyPoints.note: Use benchmarks: 10 mm = 1 cm, a school ruler = 30 cm, 100 cm = 1 m.
Compare with a 30 cm school ruler: a birthday card is a bit more than half the length of a 30 cm ruler.

steps.explain: Convert 18 mm to centimetres: 18 mm = 1.8 cm, about the width of a fingernail — too small for a birthday card.

steps.explain: Check 18 cm: 18 cm is a little over half of a 30 cm school ruler, which is the exact size of a standard birthday card.

steps.explain: Check 18 m and 18 km: 18 m is longer than a bus, and 18 km is a town-to-town distance — far too large.
steps.work: \(18\text{ m and } 18\text{ km are far too large}\)

steps.explain: Therefore, 18 cm is the best estimate for the length of a birthday card.
